Because if you think about how AI systems are gonna be used in the future, they're not gonna be in isolation. There's always gonna be a human interacting with the systems at some level, right? This was always something we put off before because the model was just not good enough.

Right? You're like, "Oh, why are you talking about human-AI interaction when the AI can't even do two things," right? But I think we're in this phase now where that's gonna be critical, and that just means that all your evals are not just going to be like "Hey, I collected a data set, and it's a static data set, and I just run the model through it." We have to have more dynamic evals. And I think that's where these kind of like simulations are where, where you're basically having dynamic interactions between different models. It can be as simple as a user simulator or it could be more competitive, like multi-agent cooperative or competitive multi-agent systems and all that. So there's this whole, like, spectrum where you can slide the slider. But I think that's definitely the way that we're gonna go in the future, right?

And in the future we'll also have humans ideally interacting with the systems live, right? And having that be part of the eval. But that requires a different skill.

astra.text:
Yeah. So I think there’s a whole range of things in between where you’re still working on a computer, but you’re not necessarily writing code, right? And I don’t think you need to evaluate an entire job at once. You can start with specific tasks that are useful within that job.

So take your accounting example. If you’re asking a system to work with some records and produce a spreadsheet, there might be things you can check pretty precisely. Did it use the right information? Do the numbers add up? Did it satisfy the constraints you gave it? But then there are other things, like, did it ask you for clarification when something was missing? Those require looking at the interaction, not just the final spreadsheet, right?

And actually, even with coding, running the tests is a really useful signal, but it’s only as good as the tests you have. So I wouldn’t say that problem is completely solved there either. You always have to think about what your evaluation is capturing and what it’s leaving out.

I think the interesting challenge is getting enough of the real environment into the benchmark. What information does the person have access to? What tools do they use? What decisions do they have to make? That’s where working with people who actually do these tasks becomes really valuable. Otherwise, it’s easy to create something that looks like accounting to an AI researcher but doesn’t really capture what makes the work difficult.

And this connects back to the simulation point. You don’t necessarily want to just hand the model all the information in one prompt. Maybe it needs to talk to someone, discover that something is missing, go back and revise what it did. I think those kinds of tasks, where communication and action are intertwined, are a really interesting direction beyond coding.

sol.text:
Yeah, exactly. And I think there’s really a spectrum here, right? On one end you have code, where the environment is digital and you can often execute the output and get a relatively crisp signal. On the other end you have these physical, continuous tasks where even building the simulation with enough fidelity is a major research problem. In the middle, there are lots of knowledge-work tasks—accounting, customer support, travel planning, maybe operating enterprise software—where the agent takes actions in a digital environment, but correctness is not captured by one unit test.

And I think those are especially interesting for benchmarks. You need to construct an environment, give the agent realistic tools and policies, and then evaluate not only whether it reached the final state, but whether it followed the right process. Did it ask the user for missing information? Did it respect permissions? Did it avoid making an irreversible action without confirmation? That’s partly the motivation behind these conversational and dynamic evaluations: the task changes based on what the agent says and what the simulated user says back.

The difficult part is fidelity. If your simulation is too simple, the agent learns to exploit the benchmark rather than perform the real job. If your grader only checks the final outcome, it can miss serious mistakes along the way. And if everything is judged qualitatively, then it becomes hard to reproduce and compare results. So I think the opportunity is to find domains in that middle ground where we can build realistic interactive environments and still define meaningful, reasonably objective success criteria. There are many more of those domains than just coding, and I expect that’s where a lot of the next generation of agent benchmarks will go.

opus.text:
Yeah, and I think the physical stuff is actually the easy case to reason about, in a weird way, because at least you know what you're missing, right? You need a simulator, you need the sim-to-real gap to close, people are grinding on that.

The middle is much more interesting to me, and I think the framing that's more useful is not "how technical is the job." It's "how cheap is your verifier." Coding just got extremely lucky here, right? Somebody already built the verifier. It's called a test suite. It's called a compiler. You didn't have to invent anything, it was sitting there in the repo. And that's why SWE-bench was even possible, right? We didn't do anything clever. We just found a place where ground truth already existed at scale.

So then the question for accounting, for legal, for consulting, for a lot of medicine, is, like, where's the residue? What's the part of that job that leaves behind some state you can actually check? And I think that's the trick with Tau-bench, honestly. The conversation is totally open-ended, you can't grade it token by token. But at the end of it, the database is in some state, right? The refund either happened or it didn't. The flight got rebooked to the right thing or it didn't. So you take this fundamentally unverifiable thing and you find the verifiable shadow of it. I think a lot of these domains have that, and nobody's gone looking.

The two things that I think are genuinely hard, though. One is process versus outcome. In a lot of these jobs, getting the right answer the wrong way is a failure, right? If an agent gives the customer the refund but violated three policies to do it, that's not a success, that's a liability. And most of our benchmarks have no notion of that.

And the second one, which I think is the real gap, is that in almost every real job nobody hands you the task. There's no issue filed. Half the work is figuring out what the work is. And every benchmark we have, including ours, hands the model a well-specified problem and says go. I don't think we have a good story for that yet, and I'd love for someone to just go build it.

grok.text:
Yeah, so that’s one end of the spectrum, right? Physical, continuous, you need a simulator, you need robots, all of that. Coding sits at the other end, where everything is discrete and text, and you can just run the tests and get a pretty clean pass or fail. What’s in the middle is, I think, most of actual knowledge work. Accounting, legal, customer support, operations, like back-office stuff. It’s digital, so you can still sit at a computer and do it, but you don’t get that nice unit-test signal.

And that’s exactly why those benchmarks are harder. With SWE-bench, the environment is the repo, the tests are already there, GitHub gave you this huge corpus of real tasks. For accounting, that corpus does not just sit on the internet waiting for you, right? You have to build the books, the tax rules, the tools, the messy documents, and then you have to decide what “correct” even means. It’s not just “did the code compile.” It’s “did they follow the policy, did they update the right records, did they ask the right clarifying question, is the final state of the world consistent.” A lot of judgment.

That’s actually the pattern we were going for with Tau Bench, right? Customer support is very much in that middle. You have a database, you have tools, you have policies, the user is underspecified, and you can still check whether the world ended up in the right state even if the conversation itself is open-ended. I think that generalizes. If you wanted an accounting benchmark, you’d simulate the ledger, the rules, the forms, maybe a user or a client who’s giving you incomplete information, and then you score the final books, not the vibe of the conversation.

The hard parts are fidelity and expertise. If the environment is too toy, the models look great and it doesn’t transfer. If you make it realistic, you basically need domain experts in the loop, not just CS people inventing tasks. And then eval itself gets messy because success is partial, long-horizon, stateful, sometimes subjective. I think people are starting to do this in legal and finance and science, but compared to coding we’re still pretty early. Which is also why I think it’s worth doing. Most of the economy is not software engineering. If we only evaluate coding, we’re just going to overfit to coding.

gemini.text:
Right. And I think if you look at the digital space in the middle—whether it's accounting or other enterprise workflows—the real challenge compared to coding is how you evaluate them. With software engineering, like you said, it's relatively clean: you run the unit tests, and either the code passes or it doesn't. 

But for these other domains, it's much more open-ended. You don't just have a static script or a binary pass/fail test. It involves interacting with complex software, using tools, and especially interacting with people. That's really why we've been looking at things like WebShop and Tau Bench, because you need environments that can capture those dynamic interactions and user simulation. When there's a human in the loop, you can't just evaluate the system in isolation or rely on a static dataset. So I think the big challenge for those middle tasks is building high-fidelity, dynamic simulations where you can actually measure whether the agent is reliably accomplishing the task and handling real-world ambiguity.

kimi.text:
Mm-hmm. Yeah, so I think on the physical end it's, like, obviously valuable, but the hard problem there is kind of well known, right? It's the sim-to-real gap. Like, you can simulate a robot in a warehouse and it'll do great, and then you put it on an actual floor and the friction is different, the boxes are crumpled in weird ways, and everything falls apart. So evaluation there is tricky because passing your simulation doesn't guarantee passing reality, right? That's kind of an open problem for the robotics folks.

But I think the middle ground that you're pointing at is actually the most interesting thing right now, right? Like, the whole world of knowledge work sits between pure code and pure physical stuff. And the nice thing is that a lot of these jobs, even though they feel fuzzy, have a verifiable core if you design the environment carefully. So take customer support, right, like in Tau Bench — the conversation itself is open-ended, the model can say anything, but at the end of the day, success is a database state. Did you actually refund the order? Did you change the flight correctly? Did you follow the policy in doing it? So the insight is, like, don't evaluate the transcript, evaluate the state of the world after the interaction, right? And I think the same principle applies to accounting, or operations, or a lot of these back-office things. There's ledgers, there's records, there's API calls, right? If you can model that state well, you suddenly have ground truth for a job that felt un-benchmarkable.

The harder parts are the things around that core, right? So like, processes are long and errors compound. Partial observability — the information isn't handed to you, you have to ask the user, "Hey, what's your order number?" That's why Tau Squared had this dual-control setup, because the user has tools too, and coordination becomes part of the task. And then there's all these soft criteria, like tone and helpfulness, that real jobs care about, and for those you're probably stuck with rubrics and human judgment or LLM judges, which, you know, have their own problems.

So is my lab working on it? Broadly, yeah. I think the direction is taking this recipe — realistic tools, a state you can verify, a simulated user — and pushing into more domains and more messiness. I'd love to see someone do that properly for, like, finance or healthcare admin workflows, right? The closer your benchmark is to how a real employee's day actually looks, the more useful the signal is. Like, that's the bar.

fable.text:
Yeah, exactly. So that's, that's one end of the spectrum. But I think the more interesting question for me is like, what about all the stuff that happens on a computer, right? Because if you think about it, like a huge fraction of knowledge work is basically someone sitting in front of a screen, right? Accounting, legal, customer service, operations, data analysis, all of that. The interface is still text, still tools, still clicks. So it's not that the modality is different from coding. What's different is how you verify it, right?

And I actually don't think the right axis is like how technical the job is. I think the right axis is like, is there a checkable end state? Right? So coding is easy not because it's technical. It's easy because you have unit tests. Math is easy because there's an answer. And then if you look at something like accounting, actually a lot of it is verifiable, right? Like the numbers have to reconcile, the ledger has to balance. So I think we'll see benchmarks there sooner than people expect. Where it gets hard is things like, "Hey, write me a memo," or, "Give me advice on this contract," where like there's no single right answer and now you need some kind of judge, and that's where all the noise comes in.

So what we tried to do in Tau-bench, and this is sort of the trick, right, is that customer service looks like this fuzzy conversational thing, but at the end of the day the agent has to modify a database. Like it cancels a flight, it changes a reservation, whatever. So you can just check the database state, right? You don't have to judge the conversation. You just check, did the right thing happen in the world? And I think that principle actually generalizes to a lot of these middle-ground jobs. Like find the part of the task where there's a ground truth state, and evaluate on that, and then layer the softer stuff, like did it follow the policy, did it ask the user before doing something irreversible, on top.

And the other thing that I think people underestimate is, for real jobs, it's not just, "Can you do it once?" Right? It's like, can you do it every single time? So in Tau-bench we had this pass to the power k metric where you run the same task multiple times, and the numbers just drop off a cliff. Like a model gets 60% once, but if you ask it to get all eight tries right, it's like 20%. And no business is going to deploy something that works two out of ten times, right? So I think for all these middle jobs, the reliability part of the eval is almost as important as the capability part. And yeah, we are looking at some of this in the lab right now. Like how do you take some of these more messy, long-horizon, multi-step jobs and make them into something you can actually measure.
